A computer has a memory system organized into four levels: level-$1$ and level-$2$ cache memories, main RAM memory, and secondary memory. Programs ready for execution are brought from secondary memory and turned into processes in main memory.

An instruction to access data in memory provides the actual memory address where the desired information is located. The information is then searched for in the level-$1$ cache. questions.html:
GO-words are sequences of letters \(a\) and \(b\) that are constructed according to the following rules:

  1. The sequence consisting of no letters is a GO-word.
     
  2. If the sequence \(W\) is a GO-word, then the sequence that begins with \(a\), followed by \(W\) and ending in \(b\), written \(aWb\), is a GO-word.
     
  3. If the sequences \(U\) and \(V\) are GO-words, then the sequence \(U\) followed by \(V\), written \(UV\), is a GO-word.

All GO-words are constructed using these rules. The length of a GO-word is the number of letters that occur in it. For example, aabb and abab are GO-words of length \(4\).

Which of the following statements is/are necessarily true for any GO-word \(W\)?

options.html: The number of occurrences of \(a\) in \(W\) is necessarily equal to the number of occurrences of \(b\) in \(W\).
In all prefixes of \(W\), the number of occurrences of \(a\) is greater than or equal to the number of occurrences of \(b\).
In all prefixes of \(W\), the number of occurrences of \(a\) is equal to the number of occurrences of \(b\).

questions.solution:
Answer: A, B, C

Suppose that we have a set of domino tiles. Each domino piece has a string at the top and a string at the bottom, for example:

\[ \begin{array}{|c|} \hline abb \\ \hline bc \\ \hline \end{array} \]

So a set \( S \) of dominos might look like:

\[ S = \left\{ \begin{array}{|c|} \hline b \\ \hline ca \\ \hline \end{array}, \quad \begin{array}{|c|} \hline a \\ \hline ab \\ \hline \end{array}, \quad \begin{array}{|c|} \hline ca \\ \hline a \\ \hline \end{array}, \quad \begin{array}{|c|} \hline abc \\ \hline c \\ \hline \end{array} \right\} \]

A match for \( S \) is an ordered list of one or more dominos from \( S \), such that if you read the symbols on the tops, this makes the same string as reading the symbols on the bottom. You can use the same domino more than once in a match, and you do not have to use all the elements of \( S \). For example, here is a match for our example set:

\[ \begin{array}{|c|} \hline a \\ \hline ab \\ \hline \end{array} \quad \begin{array}{|c|} \hline b \\ \hline ca \\ \hline \end{array} \quad \begin{array}{|c|} \hline ca \\ \hline a \\ \hline \end{array} \quad \begin{array}{|c|} \hline a \\ \hline ab \\ \hline \end{array} \quad \begin{array}{|c|} \hline abc \\ \hline c \\ \hline \end{array} \]

The tops and bottoms of the dominos both form the string abcaaabc

Consider the following set of tiles:

\[ \left\{ \begin{array}{|c|} \hline X \\ \hline U \\ \hline \end{array}, \quad \begin{array}{|c|} \hline UU \\ \hline U \\ \hline \end{array}, \quad \begin{array}{|c|} \hline Z \\ \hline X \\ \hline \end{array}, \quad \begin{array}{|c|} \hline E \\ \hline ZE \\ \hline \end{array}, \quad \begin{array}{|c|} \hline Y \\ \hline U \\ \hline \end{array}, \quad \begin{array}{|c|} \hline Z \\ \hline Y \\ \hline \end{array} \right\} \]

questions.html:
Router A serves the following eight contiguous customer subnets:

\[ \begin{aligned} &198.35.80.0/23,\; 198.35.82.0/23,\; 198.35.84.0/23,\; 198.35.86.0/23,\\ &198.35.88.0/23,\; 198.35.90.0/23,\; 198.35.92.0/23,\; 198.35.94.0/23 \end{aligned} \]

Router A is connected to above networks via Router B and Router C. Router B provides reachability to the first four subnets, and Router C provides reachability to the last four subnets.

Routing follows the longest prefix matching rule. Router A already has the following routing table entry:

\[ 198.35.80.0/21 \text{ via Router B} \]

Router A wants to ensure that all packets destined to the last four subnets (i.e., \(198.35.88.0/23\) through \(198.35.94.0/23\)) are forwarded via Router C.

Select the routing table entry that should be added in Router A to satisfy this requirement (More than one can be correct)

options.html: Router A adds an entry for <span>\(198.35.88.0/21\)</span> via Router C
Router A adds an entry for <span>\(198.35.80.0/20\)</span> via Router C
Router A adds an entry for <span>\(198.35.88.0/20\)</span> via Router C
Router A adds an entry for <span>\(198.35.92.0/22\)</span> via Router C

questions.solution:
Answer: A, B

Consider the grammar:

where \(\{A,B\}\) is the set of nonterminal symbols, \(A\) is the start symbol, and \(\{x,y,z\}\) is the set of terminal symbols, and \(\epsilon\) denotes the empty string.

We remove the left recursion from the above grammar. Which grammar below generates the same language as the above grammar?

options.html: \[ A ::= z\,D \] \[ B ::= z\,B \mid \epsilon \] \[ C ::= x\,B \mid y \] \[ D ::= C\,D \mid \epsilon \]
\[ A ::= A\,C \mid z \] \[ B ::= z\,B \mid \epsilon \] \[ C ::= x\,C \mid y \]

Some arrangements of threads and the locks they attempt to acquire can lead to deadlock. Assume that once a thread acquires a lock, it holds it until all required locks are acquired.

Which of the following arrangements will NOT lead to deadlock?

Thread $2$ tries to acquire locks $1$ and $2$ in fixed order$: 1$ then $2$.

Thread $1$ tries to acquire locks $1$ and $2$ in fixed order$: 1$ then $2$.

A palindrome is a string that reads the same forward and backward. For example, "radar" and "level" are palindromes, while "hello" is not.

The following function recursively determines whether a given string is a palindrome. The function returns 1 if the given string is a palindrome, and 0 otherwise.

\[ \begin{aligned} &\texttt{int isPalindrome(char A[], int n)} \\ &\texttt{\{} \\ &\quad \texttt{if (n <= 1) return 1;} \\ &\quad \texttt{if (A[0] != A[n-1]) return 0;} \\ &\quad \texttt{----------BLANK--------} \\ &\texttt{\}} \end{aligned} \]

Choose the correct option to replace the blank.

questions.html:
Consider the 0/1-Knapsack problem, where you have \( n \) items with weights \( w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_n \) and values \( v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n \), respectively, and a knapsack of capacity \( W \). The task is to select a subset of these items such that their total weight is at most \( W \), and their total value is as large as possible.

Suppose you are guaranteed that the weights are in non-increasing order \( (w_1 \ge w_2 \ge \cdots \ge w_n) \) and the values are in non-decreasing order \( (v_1 \le v_2 \le \cdots \le v_n) \). That is, the first item has the largest weight and the smallest value. Which of the following statements describes a greedy-choice property possessed by the problem in this case? (Assume that the optimal solution is non-empty.)

options.html: There is an optimal solution that contains the first item.
There is an optimal solution that contains the last item.
There is an optimal solution that contains the item whose value-to-weight ratio is closest to \( 1 \).
There is no greedy-choice property, as the problem does not admit a correct greedy algorithm.

questions.solution:
Answer: B

Official discussion page
